source_documents.title: Fluorescent probes for simultaneous detection of lysosomal biothiol and proton: Effects of proton receptor and spacer length on the selectivity

reference_evidence_units.quote: Table 1 clarifies that all the probes are weakly fluorescent due to the strong PET processes.
reference_evidence_units.subject: NLA-NLD
reference_evidence_units.statement: QY of the free probes about 0.002-0.003 (Table 1).

reference_evidence_units.quote: For all the probes, there exist two PET processes: a-PET from the proton acceptor to the fluorophore and d-PET from the fluorophore to maleimide.
reference_evidence_units.subject: NLA-NLD
reference_evidence_units.statement: Two PET channels in each probe.

reference_evidence_units.quote: 2) compared to morpholine, 4-(dimethylamino)benzyl is easier to be oxidized, and therefore, a-PET is more effective for NLC and NLD;
reference_evidence_units.subject: NLC vs NLA
reference_evidence_units.statement: The dimethylaminobenzyl receptor is the stronger a-PET donor.

reference_evidence_units.quote: The electron effect of proton receptor affected its electron transfer efficiency to the fluorophore (a-PET), which in turn influenced the response of the probe toward H+.
reference_evidence_units.subject: NLA-NLD
reference_evidence_units.statement: The receptor sets the pH response through a-PET.

reference_evidence_units.quote: The presence of thiols and proton respectively blocks d-PET and a-PET processes [43], and restores the fluorescence greatly.
reference_evidence_units.subject: NLA-NLD + thiols, H+

contrast_group.paper_difference: The dimethylaminobenzyl receptor is more easily oxidised, so a-PET is stronger and the probe needs both H+ and thiol to light up.
